blocks.x: Mosquitoes belong to Order Diptera, Family Culicidae. Key genera of medical importance: Anopheles, Aedes, Culex, Mansonia, Haemagogus, Sabethes. Mosquitoes have existed for over 100 million years, and only females bite — they need the protein in blood to mature their eggs.

Like all insects, a mosquito's body has a hard outer exoskeleton and three main regions: head, thorax, abdomen — with a pair of segmented antennae, three pairs of legs, and one pair of functional wings.

sections.title: The head: a sensory command centre

blocks.x: The globular head bears specialized sensory structures for host-finding, navigation, and feeding.

items: Compound eyes — kidney-shaped, made of hundreds of ommatidia (individual light detectors), giving wide-angle, mostly-shapes vision.

Antennae — filamentous, segmented. PlumoseDensely feathery/bushy — describes male mosquito antennae. (bushy) in males, piloseSparsely haired — describes female mosquito antennae. (sparsely haired) in females. Detect CO₂, body heat, air currents.
Maxillary palps — paired sensory organs flanking the proboscis, detecting odours, moisture, and tactile cues.
Occiput — the posterior head surface, connecting to the thorax.

sections.title: Mouthparts: a precision blood-feeding apparatus

blocks.x: The proboscis is a bundle of six needle-like stylets enclosed within the flexible labium.

items: Labrum — probes and penetrates blood vessels; forms the main food canal.
Maxillae — paired needle-like stylets that cut through skin tissue.
Mandibles — anchor the mouthparts against the host's skin.
Hypopharynx — contains the salivary canal; injects anticoagulant-rich saliva — the primary route of pathogen transmission.
Labium — a grooved sheath enclosing the other stylets; retracts during penetration, re-extends after feeding.

sections.title: Thorax, legs & wings: the locomotor hub

blocks.x: The thorax bears all six legs and both wings. Subdivisions: antepronotum (protective anterior plate), scutum (large dorsal plate, often species-specific colour patterns), scutellum (small rounded plate posterior to the scutum, key genus diagnostic), postnotum (contains the septum dividing thorax from abdomen), and the halter — a modified hindwing acting as a gyroscopic balance organ.

Legs: foreleg (femur closest to head, often held forward — a key Anopheles ID feature), mid/hind legs, and the tarsus subdivided into 5 tarsomeres. Wings: longitudinal veins run the wing's long axis, crossveins run the short axis — together, venation patterns define species.

sections.title: The abdomen: digestion, excretion, reproduction

blocks.x: Ten distinct segments, each a dorsal tergite + ventral sternite joined by elastic membrane — allowing dramatic expansion during blood feeding or egg development. A paired cercus projects from the abdomen tip, involved in copulation and oviposition; in females, the pointed abdomen distinguishes gravid individuals from the rounder male abdomen.

Internally: the salivary glands (inject anticoagulant saliva and pathogens), crop and stomach (blood digestion), ovaries (egg production), and Malpighian tubules (waste excretion). The dorsal diverticulum stores sugar meals separately from blood meals.

sections.title: Mating: swarms, phantom tones, and harmonic convergence

blocks.x: Males gather in lek-like swarms at dusk, detecting females by the frequency of her wingbeats (~400–600 Hz). Phantom tones — acoustic distortion products from combined wingbeat frequencies — let each sex hear the other over background noise.

Males modulate their own wingbeat frequency to match the female's — harmonic convergence. Mating itself lasts only a few seconds. Females typically mate only once in their lifetime, storing sperm in the spermathecae for repeated fertilizations across multiple blood meals.

sections.title: Complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult

blocks.x: Mosquitoes undergo holometabolism with four stages. The first three are entirely aquatic; only the adult is terrestrial. Development takes about 7–14 days, depending on temperature and species.

The gonotrophic cycleThe repeated cycle of blood feeding, egg maturation, and oviposition in female mosquitoes. — blood feeding → egg maturation → oviposition — repeats throughout a female's life from one mating event. Abdomen appearance changes predictably with feeding state: unfed (thin), blood fed (large and red), half gravid (white and red), gravid (large, eggs ready to lay).

sections.title: Eggs and larvae

blocks.x: A single female deposits 30–300 eggs per oviposition, ovoid and dark brown to black. Laid singly (Aedes) or as floating rafts (Culex). Eggs typically hatch within 2–3 days.

Larvae are entirely aquatic, legless, with a distinctively bulbous thorax, filter-feeding on organic matter, bacteria, and algae. Four larval instars, each separated by a <term d="To shed the old cuticle in order to grow.">moult</term>. Key features: prominent mouth brushes, compound eyes and antennae on the head; long lateral hairs on the thorax; and on the 9-segment abdomen — a siphon/spiracles on segment 8, sausage-shaped gills, caudal setae, and a saddle organ.

Habitats range from permanent water bodies (marshes, swamps — Anopheles, Mansonia) to small temporary containers (puddles, tires — especially Aedes aegypti) to natural microhabitats (tree holes, leaf axils — Aedes africanus).

sections.title: The pupal stage: non-feeding but highly mobile

blocks.x: The final aquatic phase — dramatic reorganization into the adult form. Although non-feeding, the pupa is highly mobile and retreats from disturbance.

items: Comma-shaped body — fused cephalothorax and 10-segment abdomen.
Respiratory trumpets — paired trumpet-shaped tubes on the cephalothorax that pierce the water surface for gas exchange; diagnostic at the genus level.
Genital pouch & paddles — terminal paddles aid swimming; the genital pouch houses developing genitalia.

sections.title: Adult behaviour: host-seeking, feeding, and resting patterns

blocks.x: Host attraction cues: body odour, heat, exhaled CO₂, visual movement, and even beer consumption or pregnancy in the host. Temporal activity patterns: nocturnal, diurnal, crepuscular (dawn/dusk), or indiscriminate.

Spatial behaviour: endophagic (feeds indoors) vs. exophagic (feeds outdoors); endophilicResting indoors after feeding. (rests indoors) vs. exophilicResting outdoors after feeding. (rests outdoors). Host preference: anthropophilic (prefers humans), zoophilic (prefers animals), ornithophilic (prefers birds).

sections.title: Mosquito species of medical importance in Ghana

blocks.x: Anopheles — A. gambiae s.l. complex (primary malaria vectors, throughout Ghana); A. coluzzii (urban/peri-urban); A. melas (coastal, brackish water); A. rufipes and A. pharoensis (secondary vectors, savanna/irrigated zones); A. stephensi (invasive urban vector, surveillance ongoing in Accra).
Culex — C. quinquefasciatus (primary lymphatic filariasis vector, urban); C. decens (abundant, not implicated in disease locally).

Aedes — Ae. aegypti (dengue, yellow fever, Zika, chikungunya — urban containers); Ae. albopictus (invasive, expanding inland); Ae. africanus, Ae. simpsoni, Ae. vittatus (forest/rural arbovirus vectors).
Mansonia — M. africana and M. uniformis, vectors for Wuchereria bancrofti (lymphatic filariasis), nationwide.

sections.title: Control measures: personal and community protection

blocks.x: Personal protection: repellents (DEET-based and botanical), protective clothing, insecticide vaporizers, mosquito nets (ITNs, LLINs).

Community protection: insecticide-treated fabrics and insect-proof housing, screened windows and sealed eaves, zooprophylaxis (livestock diverting mosquitoes from humans), insecticide spraying (space and residual — the gold standard), source reduction, biological control (larvivorous fish, Bacillus thuringiensis), and habitat change (drainage, vegetation management).

Control of immature stages is often more cost-effective than adult control, since larvae are concentrated in discrete water bodies. Approaches include biological control, genetic control (sterile insect technique, gene drive, e.g. OX513A Aedes aegypti), physical/habitat change, and chemical larvicides (insect growth regulators).

sections.title: The four WHOPES-recommended insecticide classes

blocks.x: The WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) recommends four chemical classes for adult mosquito control via IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying) and ITNs.

items: Organochlorines (e.g. DDT) — long residual action (6–12 months), low cost, largely banned due to environmental persistence and bioaccumulation; limited IRS use persists under the Stockholm Convention.
Organophosphates — very effective, short residual (2–3 months), biodegradable, low mammalian toxicity; used in larval control and dog collars.
Carbamates — moderate residual activity; inhibit acetylcholinesterase; used where pyrethroid resistance is detected.
Pyrethroids — derived from Chrysanthemum; rapid knockdown, low human toxicity, 3–6 month longevity; the preferred choice for LLINs and IRS in public health.

blocks.x: <term d="The reduced susceptibility of a vector population to an insecticide.">Insecticide resistance</term> is an escalating threat, driven largely by excessive agrochemical use — resistance surveillance and class rotation are critical management priorities.

sections.title: Bringing it together

blocks.x: Mosquito morphology, life cycle, and behaviour aren't just biology trivia — every feature covered here (siphon shape, resting angle, feeding time, breeding habitat) is a lever used in real vector control programmes. The next two topics build directly on this foundation: Anopheline mosquitoes (malaria) and Culicine mosquitoes (arboviruses and filariasis).
